A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, algorithms, figures, table, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching v2 Appendices A–B to v4 Appendices B–C.

before.justification: v2 Section 6 reports original experiments on synthetic constrained linear regression and vertical federated regression using mushrooms data, with convergence results in Figures 1–2.

after.justification: v4 Section 6 retains these original synthetic and mushrooms-data experiments and their convergence results in Figures 1–2.

M1.justification: The strongly convex reformulation, Chebyshev preconditioning, and APAPC-based procedure in Algorithms 1–6 are retained. Section 4.2 changes the explanation and notation without changing the proposed algorithm.

E1.justification: Both evaluate synthetic constrained linear regression and vertical federated regression on mushrooms data. The new consensus-reduction appendix is theoretical and adds no evaluated dataset or task.

E2.justification: Tracking-ADMM and DPMM remain the evaluated comparators in both experiments and Figures 1–2. No comparator is added, removed, or replaced.

E3.justification: The graph topologies, conditioning parameters, regularizers, dimensions, and sample counts are unchanged, including 20 nodes for the synthetic experiment and 100 samples across seven devices for mushrooms. Both use squared solution error against gradient calls, matrix multiplications, and communications.

E4.justification: The same two benchmark convergence comparisons are retained. Neither version adds separate ablations, sensitivity tests, robustness experiments, or empirical error analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Statistical reporting practices are unchanged.

E6.justification: Figures 1–2 contain the same convergence curves under the same settings. The reported finding that the proposed method has the steepest convergence slopes is also retained; no empirical result entries are added or removed.

T1.justification: v4 adds Appendix A's derivation of kappa_A >= n/2 for consensus encodings and its claimed communication-complexity implication. It also substantially revises the proof of Theorem 2: graph spectral bounds, quadratic and conjugate formulas, Lemma 6 constants, support propagation through the two-memory model, transfer to primal error, and the auxiliary gradient lower-bound construction. The main theorems retain their stated asymptotic rates.

C1.justification: The abstract and main contribution statement retain the same claims: matching lower complexity bounds and an optimal first-order method for smooth, strongly convex optimization with general affine coupled constraints. The claimed novelty and main convergence guarantees are unchanged.

C2.justification: v4 Appendix A newly argues that general coupled-constraint methods incur at least a sqrt(n) communication penalty relative to specialized optimal consensus methods. v2 discusses the reduction and communication-friendly structure but does not state this limitation. Interpretation of the experiments is unchanged.

D1.justification: The algorithm pseudocode, parameter prescriptions, CPU/RAM specification, regularization values, and data-generation details are retained. No new implementation instructions or code/data access information are supplied.

R1.justification: Bibliography membership is unchanged, but Section 2 revises the reported complexity expressions for Doan and Olshevsky (2017) and Nedic et al. (2018), and explicitly attributes primal consensus algorithms to Kovalev et al. (2020). Appendix A adds a comparison with the specialized consensus optimum.

P1.justification: Sections 2 and 4.2 receive localized rewrites, and the lower-bound exposition is expanded. v4 also adds acknowledgments, updates affiliations, and inserts the new appendix while preserving the main narrative and section sequence.

P2.justification: v4 adopts ICLR formatting with stacked author information, running headers, different heading typography, and reflowed algorithms, proofs, and figures. Figures 1–2 retain their plots, axes, legends, and captions, and Table 1 retains its structure.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses gaps in v2's lower-bound presentation through revised graph scaling and an explicit connection between the two-memory model and primal error. However, new Appendix A applies Theorem 2's existential worst-case lower bound to every consensus encoding without establishing that the hard instances satisfy consensus constraints. The proof and explanatory gains therefore coexist with an unsupported new applicability claim, preventing a reliable judgment of the net quality improvement.
